docs.text: GAWP: Germline Analysis with Pandas GAWP is a rewrite and extension of the original Germline Analysis Pipeline (GAP) from the Libuda Lab at the University of Oregon. 1 Our main goal for developing a new script was that we wanted a version that was written in Python and that allowed users to run the code either from the command line or a Jupyter notebook. We also wanted to make it easier for users to adapt the script for new projects. The result is a new organization based on plugins . GAWP has a set of independent modules that perform individual steps of the analysis pipeline. Before running GAWP, users create a configuration file that tells the system the plugins to use and thus which steps to run. The configuration file specifies the sheets from the Imaris output that have the data to use, which columns on those sheets have the relevant data, and various other parameters. The end result is that no settings are "hard wired" into the code -- everything is defined in the configuration file. This should make it easier for new users in the future to run the code on their own data sets (and potentially make it easier to adapt to new data formats from different versions of Imaris). Road Map The sidebar to the left shows the major sections of the documentation. Installation explains how to install GAWP using pip (Python's package installer) Overview has a high-level description of what each plugin does and how to configure a notebook or script to use plugins Plugin Reference has a detailed description of each plugin, along with a complete list of all the options Developer has documentation for people who want to dig in to the Python code Toraason, Erik, Victoria L. Adler, Nicole A. Kurhanewicz, et al. “Automated and Customizable Quantitative Image Analysis of Whole Caenorhabditis Elegans Germlines.” Genetics 217, no. 3 (2021): iyab010. https://doi.org/10.1093/genetics/iyab010. ↩

docs.text: Configuring Plugins At the beginning of each session, either in one of the first few code cells in a notebook or when initializing a command line script, GAWP will read a configuration that specifies which plugins to use. TOML Configurations are written in a simple language named TOML . A configuration is divided into sections . A section begins with a header that has the section name enclosed in brackets. Below that are the specifications, which look like Python assignment statements: an option name, an equal sign, and the value for that option. Values can be integers, strings, or lists. In a GAWP configuration section headers are plugin names . to include a plugin in your workflow, add a section with that name to your configuration some plugins have required settings, and these need to be included in that section other settings are optional; if you leave them out GAWP will use the default value for that setting. An important point to remember: if you want to use a plugin it must appear in the configuration . You might be happy to use the default value for all the options, in which case there will be no settings in that section, but you still need to include the section header. Here is a simple example of a GAWP configuration written in TOML. This workflow will use Geometry and both of its submodules, Foci and Measurements, to linearize a germline. [geometry] sheet_name = 'Position' category_column = 'Category' x_coord = 'Position X' y_coord = 'Position Y' [geometry.foci] [geometry.measurements] The geometry section tells GAWP which sheet has position data and which columns on that sheet have the coordinates of foci and other objects. The geometry.foci and geometry.measurements sections tell GAWP to install these plugins and use the default settings. Configuration Cells in Jupyter Notebooks To run GAWP from a Jupyter notebook: import the GAWP modules that implement the plugins create a piece of text that has the TOML specification pass that specification to the GAWP function that installs the plugins Here are some examples from a workflow that will use the Geometry plugin. Imports The first statement imports the GAWP function that installs plugins. Below that are statements that import the plugins themselves. from gawp.config import initialize_config from gawp.geometry import Geometry from gawp.foci import Foci ... TOML String This statement defines a string named GAWP_CONFIG using Python's "triple-quoted string" syntax, which lets us create strings that span multiple lines: GAWP_CONFIG = ''' [geometry] sheet_name = 'Position' category_column = 'Category' x_coord = 'Position X' y_coord = 'Position Y' [geometry.foci] category = 'Surface' index = ['Surpass Object','ID'] ''' Install the Plugins Finally we pass GAWP_CONFIG to initialize_config to install the plugins: initialize_config(text=GAWP_CONFIG) Configuration Files for the Command Line Script Python scripts read configurations from files. TOML files are plain text files that can be created with any text editor. The filename extension is usually .toml . gawp , the command line application installed by pip, looks for a file named gawp.toml in the directory where the script is started. To tell it to read a different file, include the --config option on the command line, for example: $ gawp --config rad51.toml run Summary: Define Plugins Using TOML Call initialize_config at the beginning of a notebook or script. Pass it a piece of text or the name of a file. The spec should have a section for each plugin to use in the workflow.

docs.text: Use pip to Install GAWP GAWP is a standard Python package that can be installed using pip . Tip When pip installs GAWP it is most likely going to add a lot of new libraries to your system. Before you install you might want to consider creating a virtual environment. See Do You Need a Virtual Environment? below. Simply open a new terminal window and type this shell command: $ pip install git+https://github.com/conery/gawp.git If all the installation steps succeed you will have a new command line application named gawp . You can run it with the --help option to make sure everything was installed correctly: $ gawp --help usage: gawp [-h] [--log X] [--preview] [--config F] {run,review,status} ... You will also have a new module that you can import into your notebooks or Python scripts. For example, the IO plugin has a function that reads a sheet from an XLS file and converts it into a Pandas dataframe. To use this function your code could include this line: from gawp.io import open_spreadsheet Do You Need a Virtual Environment? When pip installs GAWP it will check to make sure all of the libraries it depends on are also installed. Mostly these are well-known data science libraries like Pandas that you probably already have. But there are several that you might not have: Shapely, a geography library we use for computing distances between points and line segments GeoPandas, a library that allows us to put Shapely objects in Pandas dataframes Rich, an all-around useful library for creating interfaces for command line applications We strongly recommend installing GAWP in its own virtual environment . That will prevent several potential problems. For example, if you have an older version of Pandas on your system, pip will want to upgrade it, and that could break some other programs you have that depend on the older version. If you have recent versions of Pandas and Numpy and are not concerned with installing these new libraries (they're not likely to conflict with any libraries you have already) then go ahead and type the pip command to install GAWP. But if you're ready to take control of your Python data science environments the best approach is to use a package named pyenv and a companion plugin named pyenv-virtualenv . After you create a clean new environment activate it and then type the pip command to install GAWP. pip will do the rest by installing Pandas and the other modules used by GAWP.

docs.text: Linearization All of the "heavy lifting" of the linearization pipeline is done in the Geometry module. Input Data The data used by this module is typically on a sheet named "Positions", such as this one from an example data set: There three different groupings in this sheet. The first set of rows (highlighted in red) have "Spot" in the Category column. The next group (highlighted in blue) has "Surface" in the Category column, and the last group (highlighted in green) has "MeasurementPoint". The first thing the Geometry plugin does is to separate out the rows. In this example, it's going to ignore the spots, save the surfaces in a Pandas data frame, and save the measurements in a third frame. The plugin gets its instructions from the config file; for this project it looks like this: [geometry] sheet_name = 'Position' category_column = 'Category' [geometry.foci] category = 'Surface' index = ['Surpass Object','ID'] [geometry.measurements] category = 'MeasurementPoint' index = 'Name' The first section tells the plugin where to get the position data for both frames: it's on the sheet named "Position", and it should look in the Category column when deciding which rows to use. The next two sections tell the plugin to make a data frame for foci from the rows that have "Surface" in the Category column and to make a frame for measurements using rows with "MeasurementPoint" in the Category column. After the measurements are saved the plugin makes one more frame. This one has line segments formed by connecting adjacent measurement points. Here are the resuling frames that will be used in subsequent steps: Algorithm The key step in the linearization algorithm is to compute all possible distances. We can do this by making a table that has every combination of data point and line segment: The next steps are: compute the distances and add them to the cross product frame. group the rows by IDs find the minimum distance in each group The final result is a data frame that has one row for each nucleus. In that row are the name of the nearest line segment, the point where a line from the nucleus intersects the line segment, and the total length of a path from the first measurement point up to the intersection point.

docs.text: Counting Spots The Group stage summarizes the data in one of the sheets to produce counts. The process is best explained using a sheet from one of the example data sets. Input Data A sheet named "Intensity Max Ch=4 Img=1" has a table that connects spots to surfaces. This is what the sheet looks like in Excel: There are two parts to the table. The upper part has the word "Surface" in the Category column, and the lower part (shaded in green) has "Spot" in that column. The essential thing to know about this table is that unlike most other sheets, the leftmost column, labeled "Intensity Max", does not actually contain intensity values. Those numbers are IDs. For the surface rows IDs are numbers ranging from 1 to 53, which is the number of surfaces in the data set. For the spots, the number in the left column is the ID of the surface that (according to Imaris) the spot is closest to. Most spots have a 0 in this column, which means the spot is not associated with any surface. But you can see at the bottom of the figure, in row 5283, there is a 10 in the leftmost column, which means this spot is closest to surface number 10. Other spots below that have 9, 10, or 11 in the leftmost column, meaning they are close to surfaces with those IDs. Algorithm The Group stage gets its name from groupby , the Pandas operation that summarizes the data and produces the counts. The main steps in this plugin are: Split the sheet into two parts and make two data frames, one for surfaces and one for spots Group the spots according to their IDs, and count the number of rows in each group; note that the name of each group is the ID of one of the surfaces Append the counts to the end of the surfaces frame using a join operation that connects counts to surfaces using the ID column Here is what the group operation looks like: Note that the first row is the count of the number of spots that have 0 in the "Intensity Max" column. This count is ignored when the counts are joined with the surfaces. The result of that join is shown below. The yellow shading highlights the fact that the join is using the column named "Intensity Max" and that this column appears in both the spots and surfaces frames. Configuring the Group Plugin This grouping operation can be generalized to apply to other data sets, as well. The configuration section for the plugin needs to specify the name of the sheet to use, the names of the columns that divide the sheet into the main data and the rows to use for groups, and the name of the output column. This is the configuration section that was used for the example data shown above: [group.intensity] sheet = 'Intensity Max Ch=4 Img=1' category_column = 'Category' category = 'Surface' group = 'Spot' column = 'Intensity Max' aggregation_function = 'count' aggregation_name = 'RAD51' The full details of all of the options and their default values is in the documentation of the Group Plugin .

docs.text: Input and Output Jupyter notebooks and command line applications all need to open XLS files exported from Imaris, read data from different sheets inside those spreadsheets, and save results. But notebooks and scripts have different requirements. Someone using a notebook can focus in a single data set, often to explore how different steps of the workflow apply to that data. They can tell GAWP which spreadsheet they want to open and tell it exactly what they want it to do with that notebook. The results of different steps are displayed in the notebook, and that may be all the user needs to see -- there is no need to write the results to a file. A user running GAWP from the command line has different goals. They know exactly what the steps are, and they want GAWP to apply those steps to several different spreadsheets, maybe even every spreadsheet in a folder exported by Imaris. They also want the results of running the pipeline saved in a new directory, where output file names are derived from the input file names. They also might want to have GAWP generate a log file so there is a record of what it did. GAWP's io module supports both of these use cases. The plugin named IO is used by command line applications to manage interactions with multiple spreadsheets. The module also defines standalone functions , such as parse_spreadsheet , that can be called from notebooks. Not surprisingly, the plugin calls the standalone functions -- it's goal is to automate the workflow by calling these functions automatically for every spreadsheet the user wants to analyze. Summary: IO in the Workflow Every project starts by opening data exported from Imaris. a notebook will import the standalone functions, then call them to open a spreadsheet file and extract data from one or more sheets a command line script must use the IO plugin; the plugin will automate the opening of spreadsheets and extracting data Note: Although the IO plugin was designed for scripts, it can also be imported by a notebook if a user wants to work with more than one Imaris data set at a time.

docs.text: Define a Workflow with Plugins GAWP is organized as a set of plugin modules that carry out individual steps of the full linaerization workflow. Plugin Name Module Name Resonsibilities IO gawp.io Opens spreadsheets, extracts data from sheets Geometry gawp.geometry Computes distances between points and line segments Foci gawp.geometry.foci Reads positions of foci Measurements gawp.geometry.measurements Reads measurement points, uses them to create line segments Join gawp.join Copies data from Volume, Sphericity, and other sheets Group gawp.group Summarizes Intensity data to create counts Stages gawp.stages Assigns meiotic stage names to foci Each application decides which of these plugins to install. A minimal workflow might use only Geometry, Foci, and Join in order to create a table that has positions of cells and their attributes, skipping the linearization step. At the other extreme, a project can use all of the plugins to implement the full linearization pipeline. This Overview section has short descriptions of each plugin and examples of workflows that use them. Complete details are in the Plugins section.
